title: Immune signals reach neurons
objective: Explain how cytokines act on sensory neurons that carry their receptors.

steps.title: The reverse direction
steps.body: Immunity also talks back to neurons. **[[cytokine|Cytokines]]** released during inflammation act on sensory neurons that carry the matching receptors, changing how those neurons behave. This is the immune→neuron half of the two-way conversation.

steps.prompt: What lets a specific cytokine act on a specific sensory neuron?
options: The neuron expressing that cytokine's receptor
The neuron physically engulfing the cytokine
The neuron being damaged, so the cytokine can get inside it
A direct synapse from the immune cell onto the axon
steps.explanation: As always, signaling needs a receptor on the target. Sensory neurons expressing cytokine receptors can be acted on directly.

variants.setup: A cytokine floods inflamed tissue; one neuron responds, another doesn't.
options: Only the responder expresses that cytokine's receptor
Only the responder is able to conduct signals at all
Only the responder is capable of making antibodies
variants.reveal: The responding neuron carries the receptor for that cytokine.

steps.title: Not just background
steps.body: These immune signals don't merely coexist with neurons — they actively reset neuronal excitability, which links inflammation directly to how things feel (the next lesson).

sources.citation: Wallrapp A & Chiu IM, 2024, Annu Rev Immunol
sources.note: Review of bidirectional neuroimmune interactions in the intestine.
